tagline.text: The symbol of Philippine surfing, with a boardwalk over the reef and hollow barrels

location.label: Location
location.text: Catangnan area, General Luna, Siargao Island (about 5 km from the General Luna center)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,000 (per person, covering entrance fee, a lesson and meals)

children.text: Cloud 9 is a hollow right-hand wave that breaks over the reef in General Luna, Siargao. It is the most famous surf spot in the Philippines, and a wooden boardwalk reaching out from the shore lets you watch the waves up close.

Cloud 9 is a surf spot on the coast of General Luna on Siargao Island. Wikipedia describes the wave as a "hollow, right-hand reef break." It rises thick over the reef and breaks into a hollow barrel, which is why it is presented as a wave that professional surfers from around the world want to ride at least once. It lies about
5km
from the center of General Luna.

You do not have to surf to enjoy it. Walking along the wooden boardwalk that stretches over the shallow reef gets you as close as possible to the surfers on the wave. Sources give the boardwalk's length as anything from about
to
, and a viewing tower stands at its end. On the beach side, restaurants, bars and board rental shops sit in the shade of palm trees, so the place is worth a day even when the surf is flat.

There are two stories about the name. Wikipedia says the photographer John Seaton Callahan visited with surfers in September 1992 and named the wave after the Cloud 9 chocolate bars sold in General Luna. Locals, on the other hand, say the wave takes the shape of a 9 as it rises and breaks, or that visitors feel as if they are walking on clouds amid the sunrise and sunset scenery. In 1993 the governor and the mayor improved access to the break and held the first Siargao Surfing Classic, and the Siargao International Surfing Cup has been held here since 1996.

A bit of surfing history makes the boardwalk walk more fun. According to Wikipedia, surfing on Siargao began around 1980 when Tony Arruza and Steve Jones scouted the area, and a 1992 visit by Callahan's group drew the attention of international surf media. The boardwalk was first built in 1996 and the original viewing tower in 2003. The surfing cup was suspended in 2020 and 2021 because of COVID-19. In December 2021, Typhoon Rai (known locally as Odette) destroyed the boardwalk and the tower, and the boardwalk was rebuilt by July 2022 with support from the Philippine Sports Commission. The Cloud 9 wave itself, however, breaks over a shallow, powerful reef and is meant for experienced surfers. Beginners usually start at Jacking Horse on the left side of the same beach. Entrance fees, lesson prices and the condition of the boardwalk can change, so check the latest information on site.
This is a right-hand wave that forms a hollow barrel over the reef. A 2001 report put the lip at up to about
. It suits experienced surfers, and surfers gather from all over the world to ride it.

The boardwalk that crosses the reef from the shore is the symbol of this place. It was first built in 1996, destroyed by Typhoon Rai (Odette) in December 2021, and reportedly rebuilt by July 2022. At midday the boards get very hot, so wear shoes.

From the viewing deck at the end of the boardwalk you can see surfers riding the waves and the whole sea. The original three-story tower was damaged by the typhoon and reconstruction work followed, so check how it looks now when you arrive. Sunset is described as especially beautiful.

This annual surfing competition began in 1996 and is usually held in late October to early November, when the island is at its busiest. If you want to watch the competitors, time your trip for then, and if you want a quiet trip, avoid this period.

Jacking Horse on the left side of the beach has waves that are good for beginners to practice on, plus instructors and board rental shops. At the beachfront restaurant Munchies @ Jacking Horse, you can reportedly eat Filipino food while watching the sunset.
Boards are described at about

per day at shops in General Luna, and lessons with a board and instructor cost about
per hour. On days with no waves, you can also practice at Siargao's wakepark.
When the waves are weak, you can relax at a beach bar or practice at Siargao's wakepark. A half-day trip that combines nearby Secret Beach and Guyam Island is also possible.
Go to Cloud 9 from General Luna by tricycle or scooter. At the entrance, write your name and nationality and pay the entrance fee.
Walk to the end of the wooden boardwalk and watch the surfers ride the waves. The boards can be hot, so wear shoes.
Rest and have a snack at a beachfront restaurant. On crowded days, the bean bag bars on the left side tend to be quieter.
Around sunset, watch the sun go down from the boardwalk or from the beach near Jacking Horse.

The entrance fee is charged per day, so it costs the same even if you arrive late in the afternoon. Registration requires your name and nationality, and if you are staying several days, a 15-day pass (about ₱750) or a one-month pass (about ₱1,500) is a better deal than buying day passes repeatedly.
Have breakfast in General Luna, then head to Cloud 9 and enter. Check the tide times.
Take a one-hour lesson with an instructor at Jacking Horse. A lesson including board and instructor is described at ₱500~1,000 for about
1 hour
Have lunch at a beachfront restaurant. Places such as X Pizza and Siargao Hawker are mentioned, but check on site whether they are open.
Do a second session at high or mid tide. At low tide the water is too shallow for good surfing.
Watch the sunset from the beach or the boardwalk, then return to General Luna.
The direct Manila (NAIA)–Siargao flight is described as having ended in March 2025, when the small propeller-plane route moved to Clark Airport. Be sure to check the latest flight information.

Clean showers and toilets are reportedly located near the beach entrance.

Wikipedia describes the Cloud 9 wave as generally best from August to November, while another travel guide names September to November. The waves are bigger and longer then, but this is also close to the rainy and typhoon season. Beginner waves are available through the year.

Siargao has good weather and little rain in the dry season. The rainy season brings fewer crowds and lower prices, but storm and typhoon risk goes up, so leave some slack in your schedule. Within a day, the tide matters, so surf at high or mid tide, and at low tide the water is shallow and hot and not good for surfing.

rows: Big waves, risk of rain and typhoons
Surf season, and the busiest time is late October to early November during the surfing cup.
Good for beginner surfing and beach time, and relatively quiet.
Surf conditions vary from day to day, so check the local forecast and plan a mix of sightseeing and relaxing.

General Luna has the most lodging, restaurants and rental shops on Siargao. If you surf often, you can also stay near Cloud 9. Lodging is described as ranging from hostels to boutique resorts at about
per night.

On the beach, restaurants and bars sit in the shade of palm trees, and there are reportedly showers and toilets near the entrance. Places mentioned include X Pizza for big Italian-style pizza, Siargao Hawker for Singaporean food and Munchies for Filipino food that is popular at sunset. Shops change, so check on site.
A scooter gives you the most freedom. A day's rental is about

, and some places charge a little more for a scooter with a surfboard rack. If driving is a concern, go round trip by tricycle, but some drivers ask for more on the return trip, so agree on the price in advance. You can ask instructors at your accommodation or on the beach directly about lessons, and some shops let you exchange boards.
The entrance fee is described at about
per day. Sources differ, so check the current price at the entrance.
The reef is sharp, so wear water shoes for surfing or swimming.
Surf at high or mid tide. At low tide the water is too shallow for surfing.
At midday the boardwalk boards get very hot, so wear shoes.
Check the currents before you surf. Strong currents make paddling hard and drain your stamina quickly.
Bring waterproof zinc-based sunscreen made for surfers.
On crowded days, go to the left side of the beach, where there are quiet bean bag bars.
When you take a tricycle, agree on the return fare in advance.
After dark the boardwalk and beach area are dim, so bring a headlamp or use your phone light.
The 2-day and 3-day passes cost the same per day as a one-day pass, so they are no cheaper. If you plan a long stay, look into the 15-day pass.
The Cloud 9 wave is a powerful wave that breaks over a shallow, sharp reef. Unless you are an experienced surfer, do not paddle out here, and practice in the beginner zone instead.
The reef is shallow and sharp and can cause injuries, so wear water shoes and use safety gear.
At low tide the water is shallow and hot, which is not suitable for surfing or swimming.
During the surfing cup in late October to early November, lodging and transport run short, so book early.
During the rainy and typhoon season, storms can disrupt your plans.
The condition of the boardwalk and tower can change after a typhoon, so check on site.
Keep an eye on your surfboard and belongings on the beach. Watch out for theft on crowded days.

Guyam Island, about
15 minutes
by boat from General Luna, is often included in island-hopping tours.
This beach is described as having slow, gentle waves that are good for beginners and longboarders. Mid tide is best, and the sand disappears at high tide.
A palm-lined road with a viewpoint, where you meet fewer people and vehicles if you go early in the morning.
